entry: Israeli historian and popular science writer. Harari, a professor of history at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, wrote the bestseller *Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind* (2011), followed by *Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow* (2016), *21 Lessons for the 21st Century* (2018) and *Nexus* (2024). He received a D.Phil. from the [[University of Oxford|University of Oxford]] in 2002. His work examines free will, consciousness and the role of storytelling in human evolution. Academic critics have faulted his books for sensationalism and speculation.

Japanese figure skater and ice show producer. Hanyu competed in men's singles from 2004 to 2022. He won back-to-back Olympic titles in 2014 and 2018, becoming the first Asian Olympic champion in the discipline and the first men's singles skater in 66 years to repeat as Olympic champion. He was a two-time World champion and won four consecutive Grand Prix Finals (2013–2016). He was the first skater to land a quadruple loop jump in international competition and broke world records 19 times. After turning professional in 2022 he produced the *Yuzuru Hanyu Ice Story* series of ice shows. The [[2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami|2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami]] struck his hometown of [[Sendai]] when he was 16, and since then he has donated more than $3 million USD to reconstruction and disaster prevention.

French fashion designer. Born in [[Oran]], Algeria, to a French family, Saint Laurent won a design contest in Paris in 1954 and joined the House of Dior in 1955. When Christian Dior died in 1957, Saint Laurent became head designer of the house at age 21. His first collection there, the Trapeze line, was a major success. He founded his eponymous fashion label in 1962 and introduced ready-to-wear clothing in 1966. Regarded as the last of the grand couturiers, he is considered one of the foremost designers of the 20th century. In 1983 he became the first living fashion designer to have a solo exhibition at the [[Metropolitan Museum of Art]].

Canadian-born American actress, dancer and singer. Born in [[Vancouver]], she became a Hollywood film star and sex symbol in the 1940s and 1950s. Her breakthrough came in *Salome, Where She Danced* (1945), a [[Universal Pictures|Universal]] release. Cecil B. DeMille cast her as Sephora, the wife of Moses, in *The Ten Commandments* (1956). She played Lily Munster in the CBS sitcom *The Munsters* (1964–1966). In 1971 she introduced "I'm Still Here" in the Broadway production of [[Stephen Sondheim]]'s *Follies*.

City (pop., 2021: 767,131), capital and largest city of [[Croatia]]. Zagreb lies on the Sava River at the southern slopes of the Medvednica mountain. The metropolitan area had 1,086,528 inhabitants at the 2021 census. Zagreb became a free royal city in 1242, and in 1851 Janko Kamauf became its first mayor. The city is divided into 17 city districts. It is the seat of the central government and almost all ministries, and almost all of Croatia's largest companies, media outlets and scientific institutions have their headquarters there. Zagreb is the country's most important transport hub, where [[Central Europe]], the Mediterranean and Southeast Europe meet. The Globalization and World Cities Research Network rates it a "Beta-" [[Global city|global city]].

Mountain range in West Asia. The Zagros Mountains extend about 1,600 km (990 miles) from southeastern [[Turkey]] through northern [[Iraq]] and western [[Iran]] to the [[Strait of Hormuz]]. The highest point is Mount Dena, at 4,409 m (14,465 ft). The range formed through the collision of the Eurasian and Arabian plates, mainly during the [[Miocene]], about 25 to 5 million years ago, which folded sedimentary rocks deposited from the [[Paleozoic]] onward. Erosion removed softer rocks and left harder ones such as limestone and dolomite, forming the linear ridges. The folded rocks trap large petroleum deposits, and the Zagros is an important area for oil production.

Iraqi-born British architect and designer. Hadid was born in [[Baghdad]] and studied mathematics at the American University of Beirut before enrolling in 1972 at the Architectural Association School of Architecture in [[London]]. She adopted painting as a design tool and abstraction as a method, drawing on Suprematism and the Russian avant-garde. Her major works include the London Aquatics Centre for the 2012 Olympics, the Broad Art Museum, Rome's MAXXI Museum and the Guangzhou Opera House. She was the first woman to receive the Pritzker Architecture Prize, in 2004, and won the Stirling Prize in 2010 and 2011. In 2012 [[Elizabeth II]] made her a Dame for services to architecture. [[The Guardian|The Guardian]] called her the "Queen of Curves". Several buildings, including the Daxing International Airport in [[Beijing]], were still under construction at the time of her death.

Former country in Central Africa, ruled by [[Mobutu Sese Seko]] from 1965 to 1997. Officially the Republic of Zaire from 1971, it was the third-largest country in Africa by area and the most populous Francophone country on the continent. During the Cold War the United States and its allies supported Mobutu's regime as a counterweight to Soviet influence. Mobutu seized power in a 1965 coup and ran a one-party military dictatorship. Corruption and mismanagement deepened. In 1996 Laurent-Désiré Kabila led a rebellion, Mobutu fled, and in 1997 the name [[Democratic Republic of the Congo|Democratic Republic of the Congo]] was restored.

River of southern Africa and the continent's fourth-longest river. The 2,574 km (1,599 mi) Zambezi rises in [[Zambia]], flows through [[Angola]], forms borders with [[Namibia]] and [[Botswana]], and runs along the border between Zambia and [[Zimbabwe]] before crossing [[Mozambique]] to the [[Indian Ocean]]. It is the longest east-flowing river in Africa and the largest flowing from the continent into the Indian Ocean. Its drainage basin covers 1,390,000 sq km (540,000 sq mi), slightly less than half the Nile's. The [[Victoria Falls]] is its most noted feature. The Kariba Dam supplies power to Zambia and Zimbabwe, and the Cahora Bassa Dam in Mozambique supplies Mozambique and South Africa.

Landlocked country in Southern Africa. Its capital, [[Lusaka]], lies in the south-central part of the country, near the Copperbelt Province, the core economic hub. The region was affected by the Bantu expansion, and the British Empire consolidated control in the late 19th century. The territories were merged in 1911 as Northern Rhodesia. Zambia became independent of the [[United Kingdom]] on October 24, 1964, with [[Kenneth Kaunda]] as its first president. From 1972 to 1991 it was a one-party state under Kaunda's United National Independence Party. Kaunda lost the 1991 general election, and power has since passed peacefully. The country's name derives from the [[Zambezi]] river. Copper mining accounts for around 70% of exports, and the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa is headquartered in Lusaka.

Semi-autonomous region of [[Tanzania]], an archipelago in the [[Indian Ocean]] off East Africa. Its two large islands are Unguja, also called Zanzibar Island, and Pemba. The capital, Zanzibar City, lies on Unguja, and its historic Stone Town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Zanzibar was a former sovereign state that united with Tanganyika in 1964 to form the United Republic of Tanzania. Its economy depends on [[Spice|spices]] such as [[Clove|clove]], nutmeg, cinnamon, coconut and black pepper, and on [[Tourism|tourism]], which grew from 19,000 tourists in 1985 to 917,000 in 2025. Tourism, fishing and sea level rise caused by climate change are creating growing environmental concerns.

Indigenous pre-Columbian civilization of the Valley of [[Oaxaca]] in [[Mesoamerica]]. Its culture originated at least 2,500 years ago. Monte Albán, built on a mountain overlooking the three valleys, had monumental buildings, ball courts, tombs and finely worked gold jewelry, and it was one of the first major cities in Mesoamerica. It was the center of a Zapotec state that dominated much of the present-day state of Oaxaca in [[Mexico]]. Archaeological evidence such as burned temples and [[Sacrifice|sacrificed]] war captives suggests that the valley's societies competed with one another before Monte Albán grew. Monte Albán remained the largest city in the southern Mexican highlands until about AD 700. The Zapotec peoples are its modern descendants.

Emperor of Ethiopia (r. 1434–1468) of the Solomonic dynasty. He ruled under the regnal name Constantine I. His reign is known for the Ge'ez literature that flourished under him, for his handling of internal Christian affairs and of wars with Muslims, and for founding Debre Birhan as his capital. He reigned for 34 years and 2 months. Early in his reign he launched a strong campaign against survivals of pagan worship and "un-Christian practices" within the church. The historian Edward Ullendorff called him "unquestionably the greatest ruler Ethiopia had seen since Ezana", and said only [[Menelik II]] and [[Haile Selassie]] among later emperors could be compared to him.

City (pop., 2025: 699,007), capital of the autonomous community of Aragon, [[Spain]]. Zaragoza lies on the Ebro River, roughly in the center of the Ebro basin. Augustus founded the city as Caesaraugusta between 25 BC and 11 BC, to settle veterans of the Cantabrian wars. Under Umayyad rule it was the capital of the Upper March of [[Al-Andalus]]. After Alfonso I of Aragon conquered it from the Almoravids on December 18, 1118, it became the political and spiritual center of the [[Kingdom of Aragon]]. The city hosted Expo 2008, a [[World's fair|world's fair]] on water and sustainable development. Its Mudéjar architecture, including La Seo Cathedral and the Aljafería Palace, is a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site]].

Largest and most populous island of [[Denmark|Denmark]] proper. Zealand covers 7,031 sq km (2,715 sq mi) and had a population of 2,319,705 on January 1, 2020, about 40% of the country's total. It is the 13th-largest island in Europe by area. [[Copenhagen]], the Danish capital, lies mostly on Zealand's eastern shore and partly on Amager. The Great Belt Fixed Link connects Zealand to Funen, and the Øresund Bridge links it through Amager to [[Sweden]]. The Copenhagen metropolitan area and North Zealand belong to the Capital Region, while the rest of the island belongs to the Zealand Region. Roskilde was an early religious and political center on the island.

Almost entirely submerged mass of continental crust in [[Oceania]]. It subsided after breaking away from [[Gondwana]] 83–79 million years ago. Bruce Luyendyk proposed the name and concept in 1995. About 94% of the landmass lies beneath the [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]], and [[New Zealand]] is its largest emergent part, followed by New Caledonia. At about 4,900,000 sq km (1,900,000 sq mi), it is six times the area of [[Madagascar]], the next-largest microcontinent. Some geologists argue that it qualifies as a continent rather than a microcontinent.

Japanese aesthetician, actor and playwright. His father, Kan'ami, led a troupe that performed [[Noh]] and gained the patronage of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, who was impressed by the young Zeami. Yoshimitsu gave him a classical education, and after his father's death in 1385 Zeami led the family troupe. He wrote between 30 and 50 plays, which incorporate themes from [[Zen]] Buddhism and Chinese and Japanese traditions. His treatises on Noh are the oldest known works on the philosophy of drama in Japanese literature. After Yoshimitsu's death, shogun Ashikaga Yoshinori turned against him and sent him into exile on Sado Island. Zeami returned to the mainland after Yoshinori's death.

African equine with distinctive black-and-white stripes. Zebras share the genus *Equus* with [[Horse|horses]] and [[Donkey|asses]]. There are three living species: Grévy's zebra, the plains zebra and the mountain zebra. Each animal's stripe pattern is unique, and most evidence supports the stripes as a deterrent to biting flies. Zebras are grazers, and [[Lion|lions]] are their main predators. They typically flee when threatened but also bite and kick. Plains and mountain zebras live in stable harems of one stallion, several mares and their foals, while Grévy's zebras live alone or in loose herds. The IUCN lists Grévy's zebra as endangered, the mountain zebra as vulnerable and the plains zebra as near-threatened. The quagga, now classed with the plains zebra, was driven to extinction in the 19th century.

Meditation-based school of [[Mahayana]] Buddhism. Zen began in [[China]] during the [[Tang dynasty]], when the Chan school, meaning "meditation school", blended Indian Mahayana Buddhism with Chinese Taoist thought. Chan is traditionally credited to the semi-legendary [[Bodhidharma]], an Indian or Central Asian monk. From China it spread south to [[Vietnam]], northeast to [[Korea]] and east to [[Japan]]. Zen emphasizes meditation, direct insight into one's own Buddha nature and the expression of that insight in daily life. Practice centers on sitting meditation (zazen) and interaction with a master, with emphasis on sudden awakening. Most schools also keep chanting, precepts, rituals and scriptural study.

Set of philosophical arguments devised by Zeno of Elea. Zeno devised them to support his teacher Parmenides' monism, the view that reality is singular and unchanging. His own texts are lost, and the paradoxes are known mainly through [[Plato]], [[Aristotle]] and later commentators. They challenge plurality, [[Motion]], space and time. The best known, the [[Achilles]] paradox, argues that a swift runner cannot overtake a slower [[Tortoise]] with a head start, because the distance can be infinitely subdivided. Aristotle's distinction between potential and actual infinity was long accepted, and modern solutions use [[Calculus]].

Third-century queen of the Palmyrene Empire in Syria. Zenobia married Odaenathus, who became king of [[Palmyra]] in 260 and defeated the [[Sasanian Empire]] of Persia. After his assassination in 267 she ruled as regent for her son Vaballathus. In 270 she launched an invasion that brought most of the Roman East under her control and annexed Egypt. By mid-271 her realm extended from [[Anatolia]] to Upper Egypt. In 272 she declared her son emperor and assumed the title of empress. Aurelian besieged and captured her, and she was exiled to Rome. Zenobia was a cultured monarch who fostered a court open to scholars and philosophers, and she protected religious minorities.

Rigid airship type named after the German inventor Ferdinand von Zeppelin, who pioneered rigid airship development. Zeppelin's design was patented in Germany in 1895. Zeppelins were first flown commercially in 1910 by DELAG, the world's first airline in revenue service. A rigid metal framework enclosed many hydrogen gasbags, allowing much larger craft than non-rigid airships. During [[World War I]] Zeppelins served as bombers and scouts, and raids on Britain resulted in over 500 deaths. The [[Treaty of Versailles]] forced the surrender of most German airships. The [[Hindenburg disaster]] of 1937 and political changes in Germany hastened the demise of airships.

Standard system of axiomatic set theory, named after Ernst Zermelo and Abraham Fraenkel. It was proposed in the early 20th century to avoid paradoxes such as [[Russell's paradox|Russell's paradox]]. With the [[Axiom of choice|axiom of choice]] included, it is abbreviated ZFC and is the most common foundation of mathematics. ZF excludes the axiom. Its axioms describe only pure sets, and proper classes can be treated only indirectly. Zermelo proposed the first axiomatic set theory in 1908. Gödel's second incompleteness theorem shows that the consistency of ZFC cannot be proved within the theory itself.

Security flaw in a [[Computer|computer]] system that is unknown to its developers or to anyone able to mitigate it. Until it is remedied, threat actors can exploit it in a zero-day attack. The term originally referred to the number of days since a new software release, and later to the days a vendor has had to fix the flaw. Vendors may issue patches or workarounds, but users must deploy them. Governments are the primary users of zero-day exploits, because finding or buying vulnerabilities is costly, though most cyberattacks use known vulnerabilities. Many targeted attacks rely on zero-days.

Lowest possible energy of a quantum system or field. Quantum systems constantly fluctuate in their lowest energy state, as described by the [[Uncertainty principle|Heisenberg uncertainty principle]], so even at [[Absolute zero|absolute zero]] atoms and molecules retain some vibrational motion. In quantum field theory, all fields, including the vacuum, have zero-point energy. The discrepancy between theorized and observed vacuum energy is the [[Cosmological constant|cosmological constant]] problem, one of the greatest unsolved mysteries in physics. The [[Casimir effect]] and the expansion of the universe show this energy to be exceptionally weak. Claims of unlimited power from zero-point energy are regarded as [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscience]].
